Is there any benefits of using Go generics?

> Is there any benefits of using Go generics?

There's a big ergonomics benefit. Using bazel in editors is not very well supported, so anyone working on gvisor without the benefit of internal tooling can't easily jump to definition on types generated by `go_generics`.

It looks like it doesn't work in `bpf/input_bytes.go` anymore either... From experimentation, it looks like it works if `bpf.load*()` is inlined into a call site where `endian` is specified explicitly, but when it's inlined into e.g. `bpf.Exec[endian Endianness]()` the type-switch occurs at runtime. I'm asking the Go team if there's anything we can do about this.

Apparently this is https://github.com/golang/go/issues/59591.

I tried inlining `LogRefs()` into `IncRef()` etc. (`var l L; if _, ok := any(l).(loggingEnabled); ok { ... }`), but this didn't help the generated code.

Unlike go_generics, native Go generics only instantiate distinct code for different argument "shapes"; see https://github.com/golang/proposal/blob/master/design/generics-implementation-gcshape.md. AFAIU, all pointers have the same shape, so all instances of `ilist.Entry[*T]` and `ilist.List[*T]` use the same generated code, necessitating dynamic dispatch for `ilist.Linker` method calls after this change.

prs.title: atomicptr: use atomic.Pointer
prs.head: 9e0fc107b6e8e27bdfaa9208354cdedc4d15d89b

items.body: @ayushr2 could you have a look at this one?

IIUC, we are using `go_generics` package to generate code which is using Go's native generics support. Two levels of generated code. So why not directly replace the `go_generics` atomic pointer with `atomic.Pointer`? Maybe I am missing something. Is there a benefit to doing it this way?

> 

I couldn't agree more, but stateify doesn't yet support generics. That requires the first N-1 commits in https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/12470, so I was planning to send that after that PR (and this one) merge.
Having said that, I could move those commits to this PR, since there is some question about whether https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/12470 can be merged at all.

> IIUC [80913f9](https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/80913f9c71a1e72d7999f736377d8bf245f873a1) requires wrapping the atomic pointer fields with a struct and putting special `stateify` tags on them. I think that is also not a very clean interface.
> 
> We should probably add native support to stateify for `atomic.Pointer`; such that it should be able to detect `atomic.Pointer` usage and generate code using .Load() and .Store(). I don't know if the AST parser we use is capable to do this.

It's not that the AST parser isn't capable, it's that that state package fundamentally wants to register a `reflect.Type` under a unique name: https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/70f9a824dc761638488b988ebd33930569a83c65/pkg/state/types.go#L339

Since there's no `reflect.Type` associated with an uninstantiated generic, we'd need to do string matching on the type's name and its methods to discover that it is an `atomic.Pointer`.

> If not, we can add support for new `stateify` tags like:
> 
> ```
> 	ptr atomic.Pointer[int] `state: pointer".(int)"`
> ```

We perhaps could, but is that any better? This would make a poor addition to `go_stateify` because it doesn't generalize beyond `atomic.Pointer`.

> 
> If you intend to cleanup `atomicptr` from go_generics, then we could also just use:
> 
> ```
> // +stateify savable
> type S struct {
> 	// descriptorTable holds descriptors.
> 	ptr atomic.Pointer[int] `state:".(int)"`
> }
> 
> func (s *S) savePtr() int {
> 	return s.ptr.Load()
> }
> 
> func (s *S) loadPtr(_ goContext.Context, ptr int) {
> 	s.ptr.Store(ptr)
> }
> ```

We could, but that feels quite manual, and ergonomically worse than what exists today.

Before the codegen deficiencies were pointed out in https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/12470#pullrequestreview-3645103398 my goal was to remove type parameter support from go_generics, leaving only constants.

Now answering your first point:

> IIUC [80913f9](https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/80913f9c71a1e72d7999f736377d8bf245f873a1) requires wrapping the atomic pointer fields with a struct and putting special `stateify` tags on them. I think that is also not a very clean interface.

Well, I don't disagree, but haven't come up with a cleaner way of supporting generics with stateify. I'm all ears for suggestions!
A friendly reminder that this PR had no activity for 120 days.

> A friendly reminder that this PR had no activity for 120 days.

Yes, I am waiting for guidance from @ayushr2.

prs.title: Keep metric field lookup nosplit
prs.head: 13e28b4f18e9749f3f794c93c96f3a8a52867188

items.body: @EtiennePerot could you please TAL as the author of the commits mentioned in the description? I discovered this while investigating failures in https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/14502.
@konstantin-s-bogom mind having a look here?
@EtiennePerot could you please take a look? once this lands I will put up another PR to fix the gap in checkescape that admitted this use of maps under nosplit.

> For posterity, in the commit message: we are going from 12 ns/op -> 6 ns/op?

no, things are getting *slower*. the implementation is going from using maps to using open-coded binary search, but that is what's needed here to preserve `nosplit`.
Great, ty! Once this lands I'll send the checkescape fixes that catch the map use in nosplit.
For posterity, in the commit message: we are going from 12 ns/op -> 6 ns/op?

The commit message now explicitly states that the original paired ARM64 measurement showed lookup slowing from about 6.7 ns/op with a map to 12.5 ns/op with binary search, to preserve nosplit behavior.

Field lookup tests pass normally and with the race detector; Nogo and formatting also pass. The full ARM64 metric suite still hits the duration-bucketer failure covered by #14359, which I reproduced on current master as well. All builds and tests ran in Docker.

Assisted-by: Codex

Thanks for finding this out. I still think we can do better here, especially for large-cardinality metrics (e.g. syscall counters). Will work on that on my own, but approving anyway here though this might race.
Any idea why 48?

48 comes from [79b38029d](https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/79b38029d), whose commit message reports that linear search was faster than both map and binary search through 48 values. Added that direct citation to the comment in 13e28b4f1. This preserves the existing cutoff; I haven't remeasured the crossover with the current toolchain.

Assisted-by: Codex

Hoisted `targetAddr` before the binary-search loop in 13e28b4f1.

Assisted-by: Codex

Changed in 13e28b4f1: allocate `valuesSorted` at its final length, fill it with the original declaration indices, and sort in place with `slices.SortFunc`. The uniqueness check now uses `map[string]struct{}`.

Assisted-by: Codex

Minor nit on this comment: `valueIndices` is local to `NewField` and does not escape `NewField`. What ensures `v` escapes to the heap is that `allowedValues` (and `valuesSorted`) are stored into the returned `Field` struct, which callers assign to package-level vars or long-lived metric objects. For small fields ($\le 48$), `valuesSorted` is not constructed and `valueIndices` is dropped, but `v` is still retained in `Field.values`.

Changed construction to retain the pointers in the preallocated sorted slice and updated the comment in 13e28b4f1. One subtlety: a map can remain local while pointer values stored in it escape; Go 1.26.3's [map0 test](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.26.3/test/escape_map.go#L13-L22) demonstrates this. Indexed slice stores likewise make the pointees escape ([slice6](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.26.3/test/escape_slice.go#L62-L68)), preserving stable heap addresses here. Small fields only use pointer equality.

Assisted-by: Codex

Updated to match the compiler's [ASCII-space split](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/2dc996f71/src/cmd/compile/internal/noder/noder.go#L334-L339) and [single terminal CR removal](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/2dc996f71/src/cmd/compile/internal/syntax/parser.go#L169-L181).
